articles.title: South Korea's $350 Billion U.S. Investment Faces Uncertainty, With Tariff Policy Holding Firm - Businesskorea
articles.summary: South Korea's $350 Billion U.S. Investment Faces Uncertainty, With Tariff Policy Holding Firm  Businesskorea
articles.full_text:
Shift in Congressional Control Leaves Executive Tariff Powers Intact, While State-Level Changes and Congressional Scrutiny Add to Investment Uncertainty
Following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, Democrats secured majorities in both chambers of Congress, shifting the balance of political power. However, analysts say tariff policies affecting South Korean companies are unlikely to change significantly, as the executive branch retains authority to impose tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act and Section 301 of the Trade Act, even as congressional oversight increases.
President Donald Trump is expected to continue pursuing his existing tariff and investment policies despite the shift in congressional control. Even if Democrats seek to amend legislation to limit the president's tariff authority, overriding a presidential veto would require a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate, making significant legislative changes difficult to achieve.
South Korea's $350 billion investment commitment in the United States now faces uncertainty stemming from changes in state leadership and increased congressional scrutiny. In particular, the first major project, construction of the Encinal gas-fired combined-cycle power plant in Texas, could face delays following the election of Gina Hinojosa as governor. Hinojosa campaigned on pausing approvals for new data centers. With the first $2.4 billion installment already transferred, delays in local permitting could affect subsequent investment tranches.
The $350 billion investment commitment between South Korea and the United States comprises $200 billion in strategic-industry investment and $150 billion in shipbuilding cooperation. However, the only project currently confirmed is the Encinal power plant, while other initiatives, including nuclear power plant construction and Alaska liquefied natural gas (LNG) development, remain subject to further planning and implementation steps.
Nuclear power and grid investment retain potential for bipartisan cooperation, given the shared challenge of rising electricity demand driven by the expansion of artificial intelligence. The second major investment project under discussion involves building eight large nuclear reactors in the United States, with a total estimated value of $120 billion. A $10 billion advance payment is planned by year-end. However, changes to permitting reviews or construction schedules could increase financing and construction costs.
The semiconductor industry is closely watching whether the investment tax credit of up to 35%, scheduled to expire at year-end, will be extended. Texas is also set for changes in both federal and state leadership: Democrat James Talarico won the state's U.S. Senate race, while Gina Hinojosa was elected governor. The change in the governor's office could affect state-level tax and permitting priorities. Samsung Electronics is scheduled to begin construction of its second foundry plant in Taylor, Texas, in November, while SK hynix is considering New York as a potential site for a new NAND production facility by its subsidiary Solidigm. If the tax credit expires as scheduled on Dec. 31, 2026, facilities that begin construction after that date will be ineligible. Both parties have raised the possibility of extending the program, but the eligibility period and scope of support will depend on subsequent legislation.
Expanding semiconductor production in the United States and reducing supply-chain dependence on China remain shared policy goals of both parties, suggesting that pressure on South Korean companies to make additional U.S. investments will continue. At the same time, changes in regulations governing AI data center construction and policies related to electricity and water supply could affect major technology companies' infrastructure spending and, in turn, demand for memory chips.
High tariffs on automobiles and steel are also likely to remain in place. The 15% tariff on imported vehicles and tariffs of up to 50% on major steel products reflect the broader emphasis both parties place on protecting U.S. manufacturing, making a near-term easing of the measures difficult to anticipate. In response, South Korean companies such as Hyundai Motor Group and POSCO are moving ahead with plans to expand their U.S. production capacity.
The automotive and battery industries are also monitoring possible changes to state-level investment incentives and industrial policies following the gubernatorial transition in Georgia. Hyundai Motor Group's Metaplant America, Kia's manufacturing plant and SK On's battery facility are all located in the state. If the 15% tariff on imported vehicles and parts remains in place, Hyundai Motor and Kia will continue to face additional costs. Shinhan Investment & Securities estimates that the two companies' combined tariff costs could reach as much as 7.6 trillion won this year.
The possible reinstatement of electric-vehicle purchase subsidies, which the battery industry has been seeking, also remains uncertain. Even if Democrats pursue expanded support, the president could veto such legislation, leaving the prospects for a policy reversal unclear. Meanwhile, the Advanced Manufacturing Production Tax Credit under Section 45X, which supports battery production in the United States, is expected to remain in place. However, eligibility may be restricted based on ownership links to entities from countries of concern, including China, and the sourcing of raw materials. Managing dependence on Chinese materials will therefore remain important for South Korean battery makers.
The steel industry also expects high tariffs to persist. The United States currently imposes tariffs of 50% on major imported steel products and 25% on certain derivative products. POSCO and Hyundai Steel, together with Hyundai Motor and Kia, are investing a total of $5.8 billion in Louisiana to build an electric arc furnace steelworks with an annual production capacity of 2.7 million tons. The facility is targeted to begin operations in 2029. If tariffs remain in place, securing local production capacity in the United States will become increasingly important.
The $150 billion South Korea-U.S. shipbuilding cooperation initiative known as MASGA is likely to maintain its broad framework, but the possibility of building naval vessels overseas remains uncertain. Lawmakers from both parties have generally taken a cautious stance toward overseas construction of naval vessels. A compromise proposal included in the National Defense Authorization Act would allow allied companies that invest in U.S. shipyards to build up to two noncombat support vessels at overseas shipyards. The key question is how differences between Congress and the executive branch will be reconciled, following a presidential memorandum issued by the Trump administration in August 2026 that allowed certain vessels to be built by allied countries.
The Alaska LNG development project also faces uncertainty over its commercial viability and increased congressional oversight. The environmental and energy policy priorities advanced by Democrats could affect federal support and budget allocations for fossil-fuel development projects. At the same time, closer congressional scrutiny of project viability could lead to more thorough assessments of investment costs and profitability.
Grid expansion and renewable energy projects also face uncertainty amid potential policy changes. Both parties recognize the need to invest in transmission networks and power infrastructure to meet rising electricity demand from data centers. However, decisions on extending or restoring renewable-energy tax credits and related budget allocations will depend on congressional deliberations. These projects could create opportunities for South Korean power-equipment and energy-storage-system companies, although the scale and timing of potential contracts will depend on policy decisions and actual investment implementation.
Meanwhile, an ongoing Section 301 investigation by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative into structural excess capacity in manufacturing, covering 16 economies including South Korea, represents another potential trade risk. Depending on the findings, the investigation could lead to additional tariffs, requiring South Korean companies to prepare for measures beyond the existing bilateral tariff arrangements. U.S. efforts to prevent Chinese goods from being rerouted through third countries could also increase compliance requirements for South Korean companies, particularly in documenting product origins and managing supply chains.
Jang Sang-sik, head of the Korea International Trade Association's Institute for International Trade, said South Korea should retain the ability to adjust or suspend further investment outflows if projects encounter difficulties. He also stressed the need to monitor developments in the United States and ensure that safeguards established in advance — including payment and repayment terms and profit-sharing arrangements — function as intended.

articles.title: North Korea’s crypto heists are funding a growing threat - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: North Korea’s crypto heists are funding a growing threat  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
Editorials
Global action needed against North Korean hacking
Sophisticated cyberattacks are funding Pyongyang’s weapons programs, making coordinated international sanctions an urgent security priority.
The U.S. State Department on Tuesday called for international cooperation over the Oct. 31 cryptocurrency hack targeting Binance, describing North Korea's cybercrime as "a global problem." Its statement came in response to Kim Yo-jong, a senior Workers' Party official and sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, who had dismissed Washington's allegations the previous day as "absurd rumors" and "a serious political provocation."
An investigation report released by Binance on Tuesday demonstrated why North Korea has acquired a reputation as the world's largest cryptocurrency thief. The attack employed sophisticated techniques, including planting malware on an employee's computer through a fraudulent recruitment offer, using artificial intelligence to obtain software distribution authentication keys, withdrawing stolen assets in less than 20 minutes and deploying algorithms to disperse the cryptocurrency across multiple accounts.
Last year, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, comprising South Korea, the United States and nine other countries, disclosed that TraderTraitor, a hacking organization under North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, had stolen approximately $2.6 billion in cryptocurrency between January 2024 and September 2025. The group was also identified as responsible for the latest Binance attack.
The scale is extraordinary. North Korea's trade with China totaled $2.27 billion during the first nine months of this year, meaning the cryptocurrency stolen during that earlier period exceeded the country's recent trade volume with its largest trading partner.
More troubling is that the stolen funds are being channeled into nuclear weapons and missile development. The State Department warned that North Korea has increasingly relied on cybercrime in recent years to finance its illicit weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs.
Despite these developments, the South Korean government's response has appeared disturbingly complacent. Last month, the Foreign Ministry sought additional unilateral sanctions targeting North Korea's illicit cyber activities in response to its land mine provocations. However, Unification Minister Chung Dong-young reportedly objected, questioning why cyber sanctions unrelated to the mine incident were necessary. The proposal was subsequently abandoned.
North Korean hacking is hardly someone else's problem. Korean institutions and individuals suffer cyberattacks attributed to the North every year, with damage ranging from relatively minor incidents to serious security breaches. Recently, financial institutions have also faced large-scale hacking attempts, underscoring the continuing threat to the country's financial infrastructure.
Moreover, cryptocurrency stolen through cyberattacks ultimately helps finance nuclear weapons and missiles aimed at Korea itself. The government must actively participate in coordinated international efforts, including stronger sanctions, to counter what Washington rightly calls a global problem.

articles.title: Why South Korea’s Largest US ETF Rallied While Seoul Sold Off — and What the Midterms Mean Next - TradingView
articles.summary: Why South Korea’s Largest US ETF Rallied While Seoul Sold Off — and What the Midterms Mean Next  TradingView
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s largest U.S.-listed equity ETF rallied alongside semiconductor funds on Nov. 3, even as the country’s domestic stock market suffered a steep selloff, highlighting the growing importance of the global AI chip trade amid uncertainty over U.S. policy following the midterm elections.
The iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (NYSE:EWY) gained 2.27% on Tuesday, outperforming the S&P 500, which advanced 0.44%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF SOXX rose 2.50%, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF SMH added 2.01%, according to Nov. 3 performance data.
However, the gains did not reflect a rally in Seoul. South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI fell 3.59% on Tuesday, with foreign investors selling a net 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) of shares. Samsung Electronics dropped 4.15%, while SK Hynix Inc SKHY lost 5.03% on the country’s stock exchange, Yonhap reported. Its U.S.-listed shares, however, closed 2.1% higher on Tuesday.
The different trading windows matter. Seoul’s sell-off followed weakness in U.S. technology stocks during the previous session. Later, U.S. shares rebounded, with the Nasdaq rising 0.83% as Nvidia and Micron advanced 2.3% and 2.6%, respectively. EWY’s U.S.-session gain captured the subsequent recovery in semiconductor sentiment, rather than a recovery in South Korean shares during local trading.
Midterm Outcome Adds a New Variable
Tuesday’s rally also came before the U.S. midterm election results. Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, but the results emerged after U.S. markets closed, meaning the outcome could not have influenced that day’s ETF performance.
The Democratic sweep could nevertheless shape the next phase of the AI semiconductor trade. Greater congressional scrutiny of AI companies, data center expansion and federal technology spending could introduce uncertainty around the infrastructure investment underpinning chip demand. However, tighter oversight does not necessarily translate into lower private-sector AI spending or weaker demand for semiconductors.
That uncertainty matters for EWY, whose exposure to South Korea’s technology industry makes it sensitive to the global AI investment cycle. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are among the fund’s largest holdings, giving investors substantial exposure to the memory-chip industry.
South Korea is also reinforcing its position in the sector. President Lee Jae Myung‘s proposed 2027 budget allocates 21.3 trillion won ($16 billion) to AI, semiconductors, physical AI and data centers, nearly double this year’s allocation.
For investors, EWY’s advance highlights how South Korea’s technology exposure is increasingly tied to global semiconductor demand. Whether the rally continues will depend on chip-sector momentum, AI infrastructure spending and how the new U.S. political landscape affects technology policy.Disclaimer Preview Photo: Shutterstock

articles.title: Democratic sweep clouds Korea-U.S. trade deals, boosts clean energy shares - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: Democratic sweep clouds Korea-U.S. trade deals, boosts clean energy shares  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
A Democratic Congress could intensify scrutiny of Korean investments and nuclear cooperation while lifting hopes for solar and battery companies.
[NEWS ANALYSIS]
Korea’s investment and tariff arrangements with the United States face new uncertainty after Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress, a result that could erode legislative backing for the deals.
Some observers expect the incoming Democrat-led Congress to move on legislation that tightens scrutiny of President Donald Trump’s tariff-linked deals.
"Transparency in investment decision-making and oversight of actual implementation are likely to become key points of contention [in Congress] regarding Korea's investment in the United States," law firm Yulchon said in a report released on Wednesday. "The Democratic Party introduced the FIRM Commitment Act in June this year, a bill to oversee the implementation and ethics of foreign investment in the United States, as part of a legislative push to increase transparency in foreign investment."
The report went on to note that if the bill passes, Korean companies investing in the United States could face greater pressure to honor their investment commitments and deliver promised jobs.
The Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act in February, but the Trump administration has imposed duties under Section 232, which applies to Korean cars and steel, and under Section 301.
Leading shipbuilding firms, which play a central role in the $350 billion U.S. investment pledge, ended lower while defense stocks were mixed.
Hanwha Ocean lost 1.86 percent to close at 52,800 won ($39.40) on Wednesday and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries fell 1.40 percent to close at 282,500 won.
Shipbuilding cooperation is expected to largely survive the shift in Congress, with the main uncertainty centered on warship construction in Korea. Korean investment in U.S. shipyards and Navy maintenance work under the "Make American Shipbuilding Great Again" initiative has drawn support from both parties.
Building U.S. warships in Korea is a separate legal question. U.S. law prohibits it, though the president can grant an exception on national security grounds after notifying Congress and waiting 30 days. The Senate Armed Services Committee's version of the fiscal 2027 defense bill would eliminate that waiver, though the bill has yet to pass the Senate.
Defense firms are expected to see limited direct impact, since much of their recent growth has come from Europe rather than the United States. Korea's defense exports rose from $9.5 billion in 2024 to $15.4 billion in 2025 and are forecast to exceed $27 billion this year, according to the Export-Import Bank of Korea, with Poland accounting for a large share.
The nuclear-powered submarine project, by contrast, could face closer scrutiny by the Democrats. No submarine fuel agreement between Seoul and Washington has been reported since Trump approved the project in October last year. Starting in January, Democrats will chair the armed services and foreign affairs committees, which review nuclear cooperation agreements. Four Democratic senators already asked Trump in January to maintain restrictions on Korean enrichment and reprocessing.
During trading, defense stocks moved in different directions. Hanwha Aerospace, Korea's largest defense firm eyeing the construction of an ammunition manufacturing site in Arkansas and seeking the supply of K9 howitzers to the U.S. Army, went down by 1.35 percent and Hyundai Rotem, a manufacturer of K2 tanks, rose 4.04 percent.
On the other hand, shares of electric vehicle battery makers and renewable energy companies rallied sharply. The main Kospi index closed 0.62 percent higher after plunging more than 4 percent.
Hanwha Solutions led the rally, soaring 18.64 percent to close at 28,000 won on the Kospi, while HD Hyundai Energy Solutions, which supplies solar cells, modules and power generation systems, climbed 12.47 percent to 88,400 won.
Hanwha's solar unit, Hanwha Qcells, has invested more than $2.5 billion to build a solar manufacturing factory in Georgia, the largest investment in U.S. solar history. Its Cartersville plant is the country's only vertically integrated solar manufacturing plant, where major components from ingot to finished module are made under one roof.
Battery makers Samsung SDI rocketed 11.57 percent to close at 545,000 won, while LG Energy Solution rose 5.03 percent to 355,000 won. SK Innovation, which owns battery firm SK On, increased 3.86 percent to 123,700 won.
Battery materials firm Posco Future M, which provides cathode and anode materials to battery companies, jumped 10.81 percent to 181,400 won, while its parent company Posco Holdings also advanced 3.56 percent to 276,000 won.
EcoPro, a battery material firm, surged 9.54 percent to 76,900 won, while its subsidiary EcoPro BM soared 10.96 percent to 97,200 won. L&F, known for its high-nickel cathode materials for electric vehicle batteries, rallied 12.84 percent to 91,400 won.
The rally reflects a bet that a Democratic Congress will act as a check on the Trump administration's retreat from clean energy.
Korean solar and battery shares have struggled since last year's sweeping tax and spending law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, accelerated the phaseout of federal tax credits for solar and wind projects and ended incentives for electric vehicle purchases. The sector took another blow when Trump formally scrapped his predecessor's goal of making electric vehicles half of all new car sales by 2030.
"Given that the Democrats have traditionally been favorable toward environmentally friendly policies, and considering the benefits from unwinding Trump-era policies, a Democratic victory would be positive for the battery sector," Hana Securities said in a recent report. "Support for renewable energy is likely to be strengthened," it added.
The semiconductor sector, which is not directly linked with the U.S. investment package, remains mixed as Samsung Electronics edged down 0.23 percent and SK hynix gained 0.86 percent.
Some analysts forecast that a Democrat-dominated Congress could lead to stricter oversight of  AI infrastructure projects and AI trades in general, which could hurt demand for memory chips.
BY SARAH CHEA, PARK EUN-JEE, KIM MIN-YOUNG [chea.sarah@joongang.co.kr]

articles.title: Democrats sweep US midterms, lift Korea batteries while tariffs stay firm - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Democrats sweep US midterms, lift Korea batteries while tariffs stay firm  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
In the U.S. midterm elections held on the 3rd local time, a landslide victory by the opposition Democratic Party appears all but certain. As the Democratic Party, which advocates pro-environment energy policies, is projected to sweep both the House and Senate, many expect Korea's battery makers and companies related to renewable energy such as solar and wind to benefit. The impact on industries such as autos, steel and shipbuilding is expected to be limited.
Major U.S. outlets including CNN and NBC reported after 10 p.m. on the 3rd local time that the Democratic Party is projected to take control of not only the House but also the Senate. The "blue tsunami," a blowout victory surpassing a narrow "blue wave," has materialized. It is the first time in 20 years since 2006 that the opposition has recaptured both the House and Senate in a midterm election.
President Donald Trump effectively conceded defeat in an interview with the New York Times (NYT) that day, saying, "I fully accept the results. We will work with the Democratic Party."
◇ Pro-environment policies expand again… battery and solar stocks surge
Samsung Securities said in a report released last month, "If the Democratic Party wins the midterms, policies such as the Republican-led reduction of subsidies for renewable energy and the end of the investment tax credit (ITC) could be revised," adding, "This would act positively for Korean companies in related sectors."
The ITC, which applies to renewable energy such as solar power generation, is a program under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) that deducts up to 30% of initial facility investment expense from taxes. The ITC had been set to remain in place through 2032, but last June, under Republican leadership, the scheduled end date was moved up by four years to 2028. With the Democratic Party now controlling both chambers, there is a possibility that the end date will be extended again or support will be strengthened.
The production tax credit (PTC) that supports onshore wind power generation has also grown more likely to be extended due to the Democratic victory. The PTC likewise faced early termination under the "One Big, Beautiful Bill (OBBBA)," pushed through last July by the Trump administration and Republicans. OBBBA is a bill that significantly revises or moves up the expiration of renewable energy tax credit programs contained in the existing IRA.
Samsung Securities analyzed, "If the Democratic victory changes the makeup of Congress, we can look forward to easing the schedule for ending subsidies or readjusting support measures for renewable energy," adding, "If expectations for policy changes grow, new project development will also resume."
Many also expect the battery industry to benefit. The Democratic Party, through an energy agenda released in May, outlined plans to expand investment in the national power grid and energy storage systems (ESS). In addition, the Trump administration and Republicans will likely find it harder to push additional legislation that suppresses demand for electric vehicles, which appears helpful for the battery industry.
Hyundai Motor Securities projected, "If the Democratic Party takes control of both chambers, it is expected to pursue the restoration of renewable energy tax credits and an expansion of ESS investment," adding, "Both Democrats and Republicans have previously toughened tariff policies on Chinese batteries, so the direction of blocking China's supply chain will remain after the election."
Shares of renewable energy and battery manufacturers rose in Korea's stock market that day. Hanwha Solutions jumped 22.7% from the previous day, and HD Hyundai Energy Solutions climbed 16.3%. LG Energy Solution rose 4.3% and Samsung SDI gained 9.3%, ending regular-session trading higher.
◇ Tariffs are an executive-branch power… autos and steel unlikely to see major changes
Industries such as autos and steel, which were hit hard by high tariffs after the Trump administration took office, are not expected to see major changes. That is because changes to energy-related programs fall under Congress, but tariffs and trade policy are the sole authority of the president and the executive branch.
Authorities over tariffs and trade policy, such as Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, are unlikely to undergo a major shift even if the Democratic Party sweeps both chambers. Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG) also said in a report released that day, "Tariffs and trade policy are areas under presidential control," adding, "In any case, the impact from the election will be limited."
There are also projections that the electric vehicle market is unlikely to rebound. The Trump administration ended the tax credit of up to $7,500 for new EV buyers at the end of September last year.
As a result, with U.S. sales of electric vehicles— a downstream industry— plunging, Korean battery makers were also hit hard. Emissions and fuel economy regulations were eased, further reducing demand in the EV market.
Hana Securities said, "Even if the Democratic Party wins the midterms, it will be difficult to expect a recovery in the EV market," adding, "Fuel economy regulations are a matter of executive orders and are unrelated to a change in congressional power."
The shipbuilding sector is also expected to see little change. As the Trump administration reached out to bolster the competitiveness of U.S. shipbuilding, Korean shipbuilders had grown more hopeful about rising demand.
If Republicans had won the midterms, the Korea-U.S. shipbuilding cooperation project "MASGA" might have gained speed, but with the Democratic Party's landslide, significant changes are unlikely for the time being.
◇ AI data centers could contract… cautious views say "Democrats have limited interest in green policies"
There are concerns that investment in AI-related infrastructure such as data centers will face setbacks. The Democratic Party has shown moves to toughen regulations on AI.
According to a poll by Reuters last month, about 80% of Democratic supporters favored stronger AI regulation. Resistance has grown over higher electricity bills and environmental damage stemming from building AI data centers.
KB Securities also projected in a report last month that "if the Democratic Party takes both chambers in the midterms, regulations on data center construction will be strengthened and AI infrastructure investment could contract."
Some also say that even with a Democratic landslide, expectations for benefits to green energy-related sectors should not be excessive. Another limitation is that President Trump could veto congressional demands.
Hana Securities said, "Although the Democratic Party has traditionally advocated pro-environment policies, in this election they were not treated as key agenda items compared with inflation and immigration," adding, "The chances of immediate, major changes are small."

articles.title: Democrats' win could compound pressures on AI spending, Korean chipmakers - The Korea Times
articles.summary: Democrats' win could compound pressures on AI spending, Korean chipmakers  The Korea Times
articles.full_text:
Democrats’ sweeping gains in the U.S. midterm elections, combined with growing public opposition to data centers and mounting financing demands on Big Tech companies, could slow the pace of artificial intelligence (AI) investment and weigh on Korean chipmakers, market watchers said Wednesday.
Although the vote counting is still under way, Democrats are poised to win control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in a historic “blue wave,” representing a major setback for U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
According to a report by the Bank of Korea’s New York Representative Office, the election outcome is unlikely to prompt major changes in the Trump administration’s overall policy direction, but could “have a limited impact on AI regulation and the pace of related investment.”
“Even if Democrats control both chambers, they are unlikely to have the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto. That limits what they can actually block or push through. So it’s difficult to expect the election results alone to have an immediate, tangible impact on AI investment,” said Yang Jun-seok, a professor of economics at the Catholic University of Korea.
Still, Yang said, a clearer Democratic push to rein in AI development and investment could become a “meaningful, additional source of pressure” when combined with other concerns already facing the industry.
“From the public’s perspective, there are growing fears that AI will take away jobs, drive up energy bills and harm the environment by consuming large amounts of water,” he said. “At the same time, Big Tech companies are spending so heavily on AI that they are taking on substantial amounts of debt. With interest rates rising, questions are emerging about how long they can sustain that level of borrowing.”
If borrowing costs rise further or the expected returns on AI investment fall short of current projections, the professor said Democratic policy initiatives could become another factor weighing on companies’ investment decisions.
In other words, tighter scrutiny from Washington may not be enough on its own to derail the AI investment boom, but could amplify the impact of existing concerns over financing costs and future profitability.
For Korea, where semiconductor exports are a major driver of growth, any slowdown in U.S. investment in AI infrastructure could have significant implications for chipmakers.
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix together account for more than half of KOSPI’s market capitalization, leaving the benchmark index particularly exposed to shifts in sentiment toward the semiconductor sector.
Some Democratic lawmakers have proposed rolling back the 100 percent bonus depreciation tax break for data center investment, which allows companies to deduct the full cost of eligible capital spending upfront. Others have floated taxes on AI use and profits generated by the technology. Sen. Elizabeth Warren has said that taxing AI would be a policy priority if Democrats regained control of the Senate, Bloomberg Tax reported.
The political risks also extend beyond Washington. State and local governments wield considerable influence over data center development through zoning, permitting and operating requirements. Democratic victories in gubernatorial races in states including Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Georgia — all with significant data center activity — could bring closer scrutiny of new projects and create additional hurdles to construction and expansion.
“Tighter AI regulation could disrupt Big Tech companies’ capital expenditure plans. These companies need to build data centers to deploy the computing capacity they have committed to providing to customers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and ultimately convert those commitments into cloud revenue,” said Kim Seok-hwan, a senior market research analyst at Mirae Asset Securities.
Delays in data center construction could postpone the conversion of those commitments into revenue, potentially prompting hyperscalers to reassess the timing of further investment. This could, in turn, affect expectations for future demand for high-bandwidth memory and other advanced chips supplied by Korean manufacturers, as well as weigh on semiconductor equipment makers.
Explore More
- Q.

articles.title: SK hynix says US chip equipment license remains valid - Aju Press
articles.summary: SK hynix says US chip equipment license remains valid  Aju Press
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, November 04 (AJP) - SK hynix said Wednesday it continues to bring U.S.-made semiconductor manufacturing equipment into its plant in Dalian, China, under an existing export license, while negotiations for next year's authorization remain underway.
The South Korean chipmaker added no specific plans had been finalized for new semiconductor manufacturing facilities in the United States, despite a Reuters report linking the export restrictions to a potential multibillion-dollar investment in New York.
"We currently have a valid license and are bringing in equipment with approval from the U.S. government," an SK hynix official told AJP, explaining that export authorizations are negotiated and renewed annually.
"Negotiations for next year's license are underway as part of the usual process," the official added.
Reuters reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter, that the U.S. Commerce Department had yet to approve export licenses for additional American chipmaking equipment sought by SK hynix to expand production at its Dalian facility.
According to the report, executives from Solidigm, SK hynix's U.S.-based NAND flash memory subsidiary, have held nearly 10 meetings with Commerce Department officials since late August to discuss the matter.
U.S. officials have maintained restrictions on equipment shipments that could expand semiconductor production capacity or upgrade manufacturing technology in China, Reuters said. The department has not formally rejected the company's application for additional equipment, while separate discussions over licenses needed to maintain operations in 2027 are continuing.
SK hynix's explanation that equipment shipments remain authorized under an existing license does not directly address whether Washington has delayed approval of separate requests for capacity expansion.
The dispute has also raised questions about the company's potential investment in the United States.
Reuters reported that Solidigm was considering an investment of approximately $45 billion to build two NAND flash memory plants in Marcy, New York, with the total potentially reaching $100 billion over time.
The report said SK hynix was seeking to increase production at its Chinese facility to generate revenue that could help finance the proposed U.S. expansion.
SK hynix, however, said no concrete investment plans had been finalized.
"We recognize the need to build a semiconductor fabrication facility in the United States and are reviewing the possibility, but nothing specific has been decided," the official said.
The company did not confirm the reported investment amount or the proposed New York facilities.
The issue highlights the competing priorities facing the Trump administration as it seeks to attract semiconductor manufacturing investment to the United States while maintaining export controls designed to restrict China's access to advanced chipmaking technology.

articles.title: Amid Stock Troubles, Is South Korea’s $880 Billion AI Infrastructure Buildout Under Threat? - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Amid Stock Troubles, Is South Korea’s $880 Billion AI Infrastructure Buildout Under Threat?  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) has largely become associated with the overall health of the global artificial intelligence ecosystem in recent months, owing to the dominance of its two largest companies, Samsung and SK Hynix. The two semiconductor giants now account for around 50 percent of the entirety of the KOSPI – and the index has become especially vulnerable to industry-related volatility due to their high market capitalizations.
At this stage, it’s important to highlight that artificial intelligence has still been an exceptionally strong tailwind for the KOSPI. Growth related to the technology’s rapid evolution paved the way for the South Korean index to more than double in value since the beginning of 2025. The KOSPI’s six-quarter growth rate between January 2025 and the beginning of July 2026 sat at more than 231 percent.
However, since its June peak, the index has shed more than a third of its value, and there’s been little sign of a recovery. Worryingly, the downturn appears to have been driven by a global slowdown in investor enthusiasm for AI stocks. Fears are growing over the seismic capital expenditures of hyperscalers, which are projected to reach $1 trillion in 2026 alone.
In the United States, investors have also seen an AI slowdown, with the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF slipping 5.39 percent in value since the beginning of the third quarter of 2026.
South Korea unveiled ambitious AI infrastructure plans this summer. President Lee Jae-myung announced plans to commit $880 billion to rejuvenate the economies of areas outside the capital, Seoul. The package will focus on three areas: chip production hubs, data centers, and robotics technology.
But the announcements came in late June. Since then, the KOSPI’s value has slipped by 35 percent – over one-third – although it’s still up 37 percent since the start of 2026. South Korea’s tech outlook appears to be changing at a rapid pace. While memory demand has remained resilient, foreign selling has pushed Korean shares to six-month lows in recent weeks.
The negative sentiment has even spread beyond tech stocks and into domestic automakers and tech stocks, which suggests that the bearish outlook could linger for longer.
This downturn has seen Goldman Sachs cut 25 percent off of its target price for the KOSPI, chopping its 12-month forecast from 12,000 to 9,000 in a note posted in late October. However, Goldman’s chief equity strategist for Asia, Tim Moe, has also provided a timely reminder that the recent sell-offs haven’t made much of a dent in the KOSPI’s long-term growth, maintaining a “strong buy” status on the index.
Even at a lower price target of 9,000, the KOSPI’s implied upside still represents a 60 percent growth rate from current levels. That indicates a clear continuation of South Korea’s artificial intelligence boom period.
At this stage in its development cycle, it’s certainly worth taking stock of the potential gains. Estimates hold that the South Korea AI infrastructure market is set to rally from a value of $2.58 billion in 2025 to $26.75 billion by 2035, representing a CAGR of 26.35 percent. This growth will be driven primarily by the nation’s advanced semiconductor market, as well as AI computing, cloud platforms, AI manufacturing, and the construction of high-performance data centers.
This aptitude for AI growth can help to compound South Korea’s infrastructure initiatives. Developments in the technology can pave the way for new efficiency brought by operational AI agents, which can identify and work toward solutions while identifying bottlenecks in the buildout process.
Critically, South Korea is earning global support for its AI ambitions. Semiconductor giant Nvidia, which is currently the world’s largest company with a market capitalization of $5 trillion, announced plans during the summer to expand South Korea’s sovereign AI factory infrastructure through planned investments that will grow its Nvidia DSX AI factory deployment to 200 megawatts. The move would see the facility at the GAK Sejong data center more than triple its capabilities from an initial 55 megawatts. Collaborators on the project, Naver and Brookfield, are eyeing a 1 gigawatt facility in the future.
The KOSPI remains integral to the scale of South Korea’s AI ambitions. Although the index has shed more than a third of its value since the summer, it’s clear that expectations remain high thanks to its high concentration of semiconductor superstars in Samsung and SK Hynix. With an ambitious $880 billion AI infrastructure buildout already taking shape, it’s important for the KOSPI, as a barometer of the overall health of the AI landscape, to begin displaying some more resilience. But with a strong domestic innovation pipeline, we’re likely to see a symbiotic relationship form as more industry innovations drive investor optimism.
As things stand, South Korea’s AI ambitions aren’t under threat. If the KOSPI can recover to reach new highs of 9,000 over the next year, we might see the nation stake a claim as one of the world’s most important emerging artificial intelligence ecosystems.

articles.title: North Korea's Surprising Economic Success: Arms Sales to Russia Enrich Only the Privileged - 조선일보
articles.summary: North Korea's Surprising Economic Success: Arms Sales to Russia Enrich Only the Privileged  조선일보
articles.full_text:
“North Korea is the protagonist of the world’s most surprising economic success story.” This was the headline of a recent article by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) evaluating North Korea’s economic growth. Rowan Beard, an Australian tour operator who has visited North Korea over 100 times, reported seeing serving robots at a restaurant in the Hwasong District—a new city in Pyongyang—and using a taxi-hailing app during his visit late last year. Roads in Pyongyang were well-paved, and a Taedonggang beer specialty shop operated until midnight. Even today, videos uploaded by foreigners who visited North Korea can be easily found on Instagram or YouTube. Many comment that the country is significantly more developed than they had imagined.
◇Three Consecutive Years of Over 3% Growth
In reality, North Korea appears to have recorded high growth rates in recent years. According to the Bank of Korea, North Korea is estimated to have grown by 3.1% in 2023, 3.7% in 2024, and 3.5% in 2025. While direct comparisons are difficult due to differences in economic scale, its growth rate exceeded that of South Korea during the same period. The reason 3% growth is considered high is that North Korea had stagnated at 1% growth or even saw its economy shrink for decades. In particular, after the UN tightened sanctions on North Korea in 2017 following its sixth nuclear test and intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) provocation, its annual economic growth rate fell to -3% to -4%.
The growth of North Korea’s economy is largely attributed to Russia. A Bank of Korea official stated, “The expansion of arms exports to Russia has increased production in manufacturing and related industries.” Due to the war in Ukraine, Russia imported North Korean weapons, which boosted North Korea’s military industry. The influx of Russian tourists also proved beneficial. Transportation networks expanded, and the construction and service sectors grew. The deployment of North Korean troops to Russia became another source of income. The Institute for National Security Strategy estimated that Russia has directly paid over 620 million dollars (approximately 900 billion Korean won) to North Korea as compensation for troop deployments. North Korea is expected to secure more foreign currency through additional deployments in the future. Funds worth trillions of won obtained through hacking were also cited as a factor in North Korea’s economic growth. Troy Stangarone, a senior researcher at the Korea Economic Institute of America, said, “North Korea’s actual growth rate may have been higher than the figures announced by the Bank of Korea.”
◇Economic Growth Benefits Not Reaching Residents
However, the fruits of this economic growth have not reached the residents. A breakdown of North Korea’s growth by industry shows that heavy and chemical industries grew notably: 8.1% in 2023, 10.7% in 2024, and 7.8% in 2025. The construction sector also saw high growth, likely due to the “50,000 Pyongyang Household Construction Project” and the “Local Development 20×10 Policy” pursued by North Korea. The 20×10 policy aims to improve residents’ living standards within 10 years by building modern factories in 20 cities and counties annually. It is analyzed that the policy intends to supply housing to the privileged class in Pyongyang and establish military factories across the country.
Growth in light industries, directly linked to residents’ lives, was minimal. In 2024, the light industry sector even recorded negative growth. The electricity, gas, and water sectors also stagnated or regressed. Kim Byung-yeon, a Seoul National University endowed professor, said, “The growth in heavy industries that drove North Korea’s economic growth was due to the boom in weapons production. It is difficult to say that this growth has actually improved residents’ lives.”
North Korea is spending heavily on military modernization. Shin Jong-woo, Secretary-General of the Korea Defense and Security Forum, said, “Recently, the quantity and quality of new conventional weapons unveiled by North Korea have significantly increased compared to the past. The raw materials used for these weapons cannot be sourced domestically, indicating that North Korea is pouring funds obtained through its close ties with Russia into this sector.” North Korea recently unveiled a new cruiser estimated at 10,000 tons and a new cluster bomb, a weapon of mass destruction. It also showcased various unmanned systems, including submarine-launched cruise missiles and stealth drones. Despite lacking nuclear weapons, North Korea continues to invest to overwhelm South Korean forces on the Korean Peninsula.
In this situation, the lives of North Korean residents are estimated to have worsened. After the breakdown of the Hanoi U.S.-North Korea summit in 2019, Kim Jong-un began a “holding pattern” while suppressing residents’ market activities. This is analyzed as an attempt to control residents who had become critical of the regime through market activities. As a countermeasure, wages for state enterprise workers were increased tenfold from late 2023. This led to severe inflation. According to Daily NK, a North Korea-focused media outlet, the price of 1 kg of rice in North Korea is estimated to have risen from 4,700 Korean won in 2023 to 51,700 Korean won last month. The exchange rate also increased from 8,300 Korean won per dollar to 69,200 Korean won during the same period. Although official economic indicators have improved, the economy residents actually experience has not.
◇“Not Sustainable Growth”…North-Korea-China Relations a Variable
There are many skeptical views on whether North Korea can maintain its current growth momentum. There is no guarantee that the special circumstances created by military and economic exchanges with Russia will continue, and even if factories are built, infrastructure such as electricity to operate them remains insufficient. The variable is North Korea-China relations. As of last year, North Korea’s trade dependence on China was 98%. According to data compiled by Voice of America (VOA) based on Chinese customs, North Korea-China trade from January to June this year was 1.5069 billion dollars (approximately 2 trillion Korean won), a 19.6% increase from the same period the previous year. Recently, the New Yalu River Bridge connecting North Korea and China also opened. However, it is too early to say that North Korea-China trade has returned to normal. While trade has increased, it is still less than half of the 6.86 billion dollars (approximately 9.2 trillion Korean won) recorded in 2014, when trade between the two countries was active. A government official said, “The key question is whether China will accept North Korea’s core exports, such as minerals, which are restricted by sanctions. From China’s perspective, it will be difficult to take actions that appear to directly confront the U.S.”
Cities in North Korea with High Growth Rates Are Darker than Those in Mongolia at Night
North Korea does not officially announce its growth rate, treating economic statistics as state secrets. The most commonly used indicator for evaluating North Korea’s economy is the growth rate statistics published annually by the Bank of Korea. Since 1991, the Bank of Korea has estimated industrial production and value-added based on data provided by the Ministry of Unification and intelligence agencies, and calculated growth rates after expert verification. Some argue that North Korea’s economic growth rate varies depending on the political leaning of the government. By changing the data collection process, left-wing governments are said to report higher growth rates for North Korea, while right-wing governments report lower rates.
“Nighttime light intensity,” which refers to the brightness of the night sky, is also used as an indicator to assess North Korea’s economy. 38 North, a North Korea-focused media outlet, analyzed satellite images of the entire North Korean territory from June 2023 to June of this year and found that overall nighttime light intensity had increased. However, North Korean cities still had 27–35% lower light intensity compared to Mongolian cities of similar size. Tesla CEO Elon Musk also posted satellite images comparing the nighttime light intensity of the two Koreas on X. While South Korea was brightly lit, North Korea had lights only in some areas like Pyongyang, centered around the Military Demarcation Line (MDL).
Recently, videos and posts about North Korea on social media have been partially cited as evidence of economic growth. However, such anecdotes have the effect of dramatically glorifying North Korea. Kim Byung-yeon, a distinguished professor at Seoul National University, said, “If there is one thing to avoid when evaluating North Korea’s economy, it is the stories of people who have been there.” Tourists only see specific areas like Pyongyang, which Kim Jong-un created for regime propaganda, leading to a tendency to misjudge and overestimate the actual state of North Korea’s economy.

articles.title: SK hynix faces dilemma between Solidigm investment, Chinese plant expansion - The Korea Times
articles.summary: SK hynix faces dilemma between Solidigm investment, Chinese plant expansion  The Korea Times
articles.full_text:
SK hynix is facing a growing dilemma over U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductor equipment for its NAND flash plant in China, as Washington's reluctance to approve equipment shipments slows the chipmaker's plans to generate revenue from the Chinese plant to finance new production facilities for its NAND flash unit Solidigm in the United States.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that U.S. officials have held up approval for American chipmaking equipment needed by SK hynix to expand production in its NAND plant in Dalian, China.
The Dalian plant is a key production hub for Solidigm, manufacturing NAND flash memory and enterprise solid-state drives used in smartphones and data centers. SK hynix is seeking to resume investment in its second Dalian plant to expand NAND production capacity.
SK hynix had its Validated End User status expanded by the U.S. Commerce Department in 2023, effectively allowing it to bring American chipmaking equipment into its Chinese plants indefinitely. However, Washington revoked the status at the end of 2025 and replaced it with annual export licenses that allow certain equipment with quantity limits, but not for upgrading technology or expanding capacity.
The company received approval to bring in such equipment this year, and negotiations over next year's permits are still ongoing under the new licensing system.
That approval, however, does not extend to SK hynix's planned investment in its second Dalian plant. Washington appears to view the plan as an expansion or upgrade, though it has not formally denied it.
According to Reuters, Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler maintained his position during a meeting last week that the U.S. did not want to allow additional American chipmaking equipment into China for capacity upgrades or expansion, though SK hynix argues that the investment should be permitted because it would involve installing equipment in an existing empty cleanroom rather than constructing a new facility.
SK hynix declined to confirm or comment on matters related to equipment export licenses, but industry officials believe the issue is closely tied to Solidigm's investment plans in the United States.
Solidigm is reportedly considering investing $45 billion to build two NAND flash memory plants in New York, with some estimates suggesting that the investment could eventually reach $100 billion.
In a regulatory filing on Oct. 29, SK hynix said it was “reviewing various options to strengthen Solidigm's competitiveness and expand its production capacity, but that no decisions had been finalized.”
To finance this, SK hynix had been reviewing listing Solidigm, but announced on Oct. 23 that it had suspended plans, citing capital market conditions. With SK hynix also facing significant investment needs in Korea, securing sufficient funding remains a challenge despite its record-breaking earnings.
Against this backdrop, industry observers had speculated that SK hynix could use profits generated by improving productivity at its Dalian plant to help finance Solidigm's planned U.S. factories. However, delays in securing approval to bring in equipment needed to expand the Chinese plant's production capacity are now complicating that strategy.
“The current situation seems to be a dilemma for SK hynix,” an industry official said. “The company wants to expand its production capacity while the supply shortage continues, but the issue is complicated by U.S.-China tensions over semiconductor manufacturing equipment, making it difficult to resolve as a single company.”
